title: Millions of Americans Discover Canadian Citizenship Pathway as Birthright Restrictions Loom
excerpt: Canada's Bill C-3 eliminated generational cutoffs for citizenship by descent, opening the door for millions of Americans with Canadian ancestry — just as the U.S. debates tightening its own birthright rules.
body:
• Canada's Bill C-3, which took effect on December 15, 2025, eliminated the first-generation limit for citizenship by descent, making millions of Americans with Canadian parents or grandparents eligible for Canadian citizenship.
  • Applications have surged as Americans — particularly in New England, where up to 3 million residents may qualify — seek a second passport amid political uncertainty in the U.S.
  • For those born before December 15, 2025, the old generational cutoff no longer applies; anyone who can trace lineage to a Canadian ancestor is automatically eligible.
  • The interest coincides with ongoing debate in the U.S. over birthright citizenship restrictions, adding urgency to dual-citizenship planning for immigrant communities.

What Bill C-3 Changed

Canada's Citizenship Act was amended through Bill C-3, which came into effect on December 15, 2025. The law reversed a "first-generation limit" that had been imposed by Canada's Conservative government in 2009, which blocked Canadians born abroad from passing their citizenship to children who were also born outside Canada.

https://x.com/canadavisa_com/status/2086770522998939848

Under the new rules, the generational cutoff has been eliminated entirely for anyone born before December 15, 2025. If at least one parent is recognized as a Canadian citizen by descent — regardless of how many generations removed from Canada — their children are now eligible. For children born on or after that date, a "substantial connection test" applies: the Canadian parent must have lived in Canada for at least three years before the child's birth or adoption.

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, the government department overseeing the process, has said it expects tens of thousands of applications, according to CNN.

The New England Phenomenon

While the law applies to Americans nationwide, the concentration of eligibility is particularly striking in New England. Demographers estimate that up to three million Americans in that region alone may qualify, stemming from a historic mass migration of Canadians to the United States between 1870 and 1930, according to analysis by Liberty Immigration.

"I really don't recognize my world anymore."

— Ellen Robillard, New York resident applying for Canadian citizenship with her son

CNN reported on Americans like Ellen Robillard, a 52-year-old New York State resident whose mother was born in Nova Scotia. Robillard first looked into Canadian citizenship when Donald Trump was elected in 2016 but abandoned the idea because her son wouldn't have qualified under the old rules. With Bill C-3's passage, both she and her son are now applying.

"Since criteria for citizenship expanded with the passage of Bill C-3, millions of Americans have become eligible to claim Canadian citizenship," CNN reported. Robillard, an outspoken local Democratic Committee leader, cited political violence and escalating threats as factors driving her decision.

A Dual Pressure on Immigrant Communities

The surge in Canadian citizenship interest comes against the backdrop of an ongoing U.S. debate over birthright citizenship. The 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution guarantees citizenship to all persons born on American soil, a principle upheld by the Supreme Court since 1898. But proposals to restrict or reinterpret this right have gained political traction, creating anxiety particularly among immigrant communities.

For Indian Americans, who are overwhelmingly in the U.S. on work-based visas and green cards, the birthright citizenship debate carries specific implications. Many families have U.S.-born children whose citizenship status has never been in question. Any narrowing of birthright provisions — however unlikely to survive constitutional challenge — would add uncertainty to already complex immigration planning.

Canada, by contrast, maintains unrestricted birthright citizenship for anyone born on Canadian soil, joining 34 other nations that offer similar provisions. The expansion of citizenship by descent through Bill C-3 adds another layer: Americans with any Canadian ancestry now have a potential second passport.

How to Qualify

The eligibility criteria are straightforward for those born before December 15, 2025. Applicants must demonstrate that at least one parent is considered a Canadian citizen by descent, which requires documenting the family connection through official records — birth certificates, census data, naturalization papers, or immigration records.

For those born after the cutoff date, the substantial connection test requires the Canadian parent to have accumulated at least 1,095 days (three years) of physical presence in Canada before the child's birth or adoption, according to guidelines published by settler.ca, a Canadian immigration resource.

Audrey Macklin, a law professor at the University of Toronto, told USA Today that applicants must be "grandfathered in," meaning their parent must already be recognized as a Canadian citizen by descent. The process applies equally to biological children and adopted children.

What to Watch

The practical implications will unfold over months as applications are processed and any legal ambiguities are tested. For dual-citizen hopefuls, documentation is the critical first step — particularly for families whose Canadian ties stretch back multiple generations and whose records may be incomplete.

Canadian citizenship carries tangible benefits including a strong passport, access to Canada's healthcare and social systems, and global mobility through visa-free travel agreements. For Americans weighing a backup plan, the window opened by Bill C-3 represents a rare expansion of citizenship rights at a time when the trend elsewhere has been toward restriction.
